title: Smart-flame-retarding layered composite Li negative electrode for safe Li metal battery

paper_content.abstract: The high flammability problem of Li metal negative electrode has persistently impeded the safe application of energy-dense Li metal batteries. Conventional flame retardant mixing strategy also fails in addressing this challenge because of the severe function-destroying corrosion reaction between flame retardant and Li metal. In this work, we propose a layered graphene oxide/flame retardant/lithiophilic ZnO layer/Li metal negative electrode for eliminating the corrosion between Li metal and flame retardant, while smart releasing the thermal-triggered flame-retarding gases for covering and bonding with Li metal against combustion. This smart-flame-retard layered Li negative electrode afford 2677.78% prolonged battery cycle life than pure Li negative electrode after 600℃ ignition, and 94.68% suppressed side reaction than conventional flame retardant-Li mixture during regular electrode operation. This resolution on the flammability challenge of Li metal negative electrode presents a meaningful advancement for safety Li metal battery construction.
paper_content.introduction:
With the rapid development of electric vehicle, portable electronic devices and clean energy consumption market, scientists are in eager persuit of new battery technologies with both high energy density and high safety characteristics 1-3. Among the negative electrode candidate materials for high-energy-density Li battery technology, Li metal stands out due to the highest theoretical specific capacity (3860 mAh g-1) and lowest electrochemical potential (-3.04 V versus standard hydrogen electrode), rendering it the ultimate negative electrode choice for building energy-dese Li batteries 4,5. However, Li metal batteries (LMBs) face serious safety concerns due to the inherent high flammability of Li metal negative electrode 6,7. As one of the most reductive metal, metallic Li can be very easily ignited when exposed to heat, humidity or air, generating a ~1200℃ intense combustion that cannot be extinguished by regular strategy (Fig. 1a). This will result in high thermal runaway and catastrophic accidents that far exceeds conventional Li-ion battery 8, posing significant challenge on the safe application of Li metal battery.

Despite this well-known severe combustion problem of Li metal negative electrode, current research efforts on safe Li battery construction are mainly focused on developing non-flammable liquid or solid electrolytes 9-12, high thermal-stable separators 13,14, intelligent response separators 15,16 and battery management systems 17. Other strategies such as artificial protection layer are also developed to improve the air-stability of Li metal to some extent 18-20. However, all these above strategies fail to provide sufficient flame-retardant effects to extinguish the ignition of Li metal negative electrode, because of the high flammability and reductivity of Li metal and failure of delivering fire-extinguishing function inside the Li metal. This safety issue remains as one of the most critical unsolved challenges since the invention of Li battery, impeding the large-scale practical application of LMBs for decades.

To solve the high flammability challenge of Li metal negative electrode, the necessary solution is incorporating flame-retardant materials into the negative electrode (Fig. 1b). However, this conventional mixing strategy is ineffective due to the severe side reaction between highly reductive Li metal and flame-retardant materials. During Li electrode fabrication processes such as molten Li infusion or mechanical mixing (Fig. 1c), these phosphorus or halogen element-based flame retardants will severely react with Li metal, resulting in the simultaneous loss of the flame-extinguishing effect of flame retardant and negative electrode function of Li metal negative electrode. Furthermore, if the flame retardant-containing Li metal electrode is assembled into the battery as an negative electrode, the flame retardant will be dissolved into the electrolyte, corrode the Li metal active materials and generate unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), which greatly deteriorates the battery performance (Fig. 1d) 21,22. This incompatibility between Li metal and flame retardants presents significant technical bottlenecks for achieving the effective flame-retardant modification of Li metal negative electrode. Therefore, no strategy has ever been proposed to tackle the high flammability problem o f Li metal negative electrode, making it a well-known unsolved problem that has impeded the application of LMB technology, since its invention decades ago.

Here, we develop a layered host strategy that layer-by-layered assembly Li metal, lithiophilic zinc oxide (ZnO) layer and fire retardant onto three-dimensional graphene oxide foam, successfully eliminating the incompatibility between Li metal and flame retardants and affording smart-flame-retarding function for addressing the flammability challenge of Li metal negative electrode. We discover that this smart-flame-retarding ability should be attributed to three key material design concepts: (1) the high thermal insulation/dissipation property of three-dimensional aerogel structure against heating; (2) effective blocking of side reaction between Li and flame retardant during both electrode fabrication and battery operation from the ZnO interlayer (Fig. 1e and f); (3) thermal-triggered, smart in-situ release of flame-retarding gases from inside the composite negative electrode to dilute air and bond with Li towards self-flame-retarding under ignition condition (Fig. 1g). From these merits, our smart-flame-retarding layered composite Li negative electrode successfully decreases the self-extinguishing time of Li metal from 979.27 to 0 s g-1 even if immersed in open fire for 10 seconds, affording 85.81% electrode capacity reservation and 93.57% full-cell capacity reservation after 250 cycles even if the Li negative electrode was pre-immersed in an open flame. Fabricated pouch cell using smart-flame-retarding layered composite Li negative electrode maintains consistent power output under the condition of direct ignition on Li negative electrode, demonstrating the successful resolution of Li metal battery safety hazard. Meanwhile, the severe side reaction between Li metal and flame retardant during regular electrode operation is also eliminated by flame retardant-sealing layered structure design, delivering 301.61% prolonged cycle life than conventional flame retardant-Li mixture. This smart-flame-retarding layered composite host design provides ideas for addressing the long-existing high flammability challenges of Li metal negative electrode for safe and durable Li metal battery application.
paper_content.results:
Fabrication of smart-flame-retarding layered composite Li negative electrode

The composite Li metal negative electrode was fabricated by flame-retarding host preparation, layered structure construction and molten Li infusion steps (Fig. 2a). Initially, a mixed graphene oxide (GO) and triphenyl phosphate (TPP flame retardant) aqueous solution was coated onto glass substrate and freeze-dried to form a porous foam, which was then roll-to-roll calendared to a thickness of 80 μm. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images and X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra demonstrate that TPP was uniformly coated onto the 40-nm-thick GO layers, generating a 260-nm-thick TPP-on-GO, bilayer-structured foam (TPP/GO) (Fig. 2b and c, Supplementary Fig. 1a to c and Supplementary Fig. 2). Subsequently, diethylzinc and water vapors were alternatively pulsed into the TPP/GO foam, absorbed on the TPP/GO layer and purged out using an industrial-level atomic layer deposition (ALD) fabrication procedure, converting into a uniform ZnO film that covers the TPP/GO aerogel into ZnO/TPP/GO host (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 1d). This ZnO layer can provide good lithiophilicity for molten Li infusion, while shielding the inner TPP layer from contacting Li metal. Therefore, the tetra layered composite negative electrode (Li/ZnO/TPP/GO) can be fabricated by edge-contacting molten Li absorption into the host 23 (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 3). Absence of TPP decomposition-derived smoke was witnessed during this molten Li infusion into ZnO/TPP/GO host (Supplementary Movie 1). In contrast, large amount of TPP-Li side reaction-generated smoke and failure of molten Li infusion were observed during contacting TPP/GO foam (without ZnO layer) with molten Li (Supplementary Movie 2). This proves the shielding effect of ZnO layer and layered structure for terminating the corrosion reaction between TPP and Li metal, so we also fabricate the Li@TPP/GO control sample by attaching regular Li foil to TPP/GO host for comparison (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Cross-sectional focused ion beam (FIB)-SEM image on Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode shows that the Li metal was filled into the micropores of the ZnO/TPP/GO host (Fig. 2f), while magnified EDS mapping images show a clear layered distribution of characteristic elements: carbon-containing GO and TPP layer inside, zinc and oxygen-containing ZnO layer in the middle, and carbon/oxygen-free metallic Li layer outside (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. 5). XRD spectra show that TPP, ZnO and Li were stepwise incorporated into the host during fabrication (Fig. 2h), converting the ZnO into LiZn without deteriorating TPP inside. These characterizations prove the successful fabrication of tetralayer Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode, which confines TPP inside the ZnO layer and separate TPP from metallic Li during electrode preparation and battery operation. This enables the compatibility between flame retardant and Li metal, which is the key to achieving the flame retardancy for the Li metal negative electrode while ensuring the electrochemical performance of LMBs. In addition, this composite negative electrode has great potential for large-scale manufacturing and practical applications, as the preparation steps are elaborately designed based on commercially available raw materials (GO and TPP solution) 24 and mature industrial production techniques (ALD and composite Li fabrications procedures) 25,26, enabling decimeter-scale electrodes sufficient for pouch cell fabrication even in laboratories (Supplementary Fig. 6). Detailed calculations in Supplementary Table 1 and Note 1 prove that our composite Li negative electrode design have minor effect on reducing the specific energy andenergy density of the lithium metal battery.

Mechanism and effect of the flame retardancy from layered host design

To elucidate the flame-retarding effect of our layered composite host design, we conducted a self-extinguishing time (SET) test by recording the burning/extinguishing time span of different kinds of electrode (using both digital camera and infrared thermal camera (ITC)), after 3 times of 2-second ignitions in 600℃ flame (Fig. 3a) 9. After testing the SET of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrodes with different TPP loading, we discovered that the layered Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode with TPP and GO mass percentage of 12.4% and 6.2% can illustrate a complete suppression of ignition, good electrode integration and constant temperature maintenance below 400℃ (Supplementary Fig. 7, Fig. 3b and Supplementary Movie 3). Even after a further sustained 10 seconds of constant ignition, Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode still illustrates an SET of 0 s g-1, defining it as a non-combustible material 9 (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Movies 4-8). In comparison, the conventional pure Li electrode shows a long-duration 1219.4℃ flame after only 0.9 seconds of ignition (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Movie 9), illustrating a SET of 979.27 s g-1 as highly flammable materials. The Li@TPP/GO control sample with same TPP/GO loading (but absence of ZnO protection or layered structure) also illustrate a severe combustion at 1127.4℃ with high SET of 744.31 s g-1 after only 0.5 seconds of ignition (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Movie 10). The SEM images of the three electrodes after ignition indicate that the layered composite electrode structure of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO was well retained after ignition, while the structure of pure Li and Li@TPP/GO electrodes were deteriorated and converted into powders due to the severe combustion (Supplementary Fig. 9).

Air-atmosphere differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) characterizations show that pure Li electrode exhibited a large exothermic peak at 475.8℃ with heat generation of 2498.61 J g−1, while the Li@TPP/GO electrode displayed a similar heat-releasing peak at 437.9℃ with heat generation of 1392.93 J g−1, which corresponded to the intense combustion reaction of Li metal. In comparison, the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode illustrated a significantly decreased exothermic peak (732.06 J g−1 at 407.0℃), suggesting the heat-releasing reaction during metallic Li combustion in air was greatly suppressed owing to our fire-retardant electrode layered structure design (Fig. 3e). XRD spectra show that the metallic Li in pure Li and Li@TPP/GO electrode was fully converted to the combustion product of Li2O, Li2CO3 and LiOH after ignition, while the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode well remained its Li and LiZn-dominant component (Fig. 3f). These comparisons between Li/ZnO/TPP/GO and Li@TPP/GO show that the good flame retardancy can be attributed to the ZnO interlayered structure we designed in host, because they have the identical TPP content.

To elucidate the mechanisms of the fire retardancy of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode, we conducted multiple simulations and characterizations on these electrodes from three perspectives. The first mechanism at the initial stage of ignition is the low thermal conduction and high thermal dissipation-induced flame-retardant effect of the porous aerogel structure 27, as evidenced by the infrared thermal mapping showing relatively lower temperature of most parts in the electrode than ignition site after several seconds of ignition (Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11). The freeze-dried porous GO aerogel structure can deliver good fire-retardancy and heat dissipation after ignition, while the dense GO film structure with exactly same composition were rapidly burned out after 1 second of ignition, suggesting that this three-dimensional porous structure can improve the flame-retardant property of the electrode (Supplementary Fig. 12, Movies 11 and 12). COMSOL simulations further illustrate that the thermal conductivity of foam-structured porous Li (1.3327 W m-1 K-1) is around 1/63 of that of dense Li (84 W m-1 K-1), while the thermal dissipation speed of Li foam is also much faster. Therefore, under a constant heat source at 600℃ on one side, dense Li presents a uniform temperature distribution of high 600℃ across the whole electrode after only 2 seconds, while foamed Li maintains a distinct and dynamically stable temperature gradient that shows <300℃ at most of the electrode even after 10 seconds (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Movies 13 and 14). This greatly promoted heat dissipation effect can greatly delay the heat conduction and the melting of Li metal within the electrode, thereby promoting the flame retardancy of three-dimensional porous Li electrode, which cannot be realized by dense Li foil or the Li foil-TPP/GO host attaching structure in Li@TPP/GO electrode (Supplementary Fig. 13). As the electrode temperature rises, the second mechanism involves the releasing of TPP decomposition-derived flame-retardant gases around Li metal to isolate it from oxygen gas, as evidenced by the observed flame-retardant gas release (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15). Two control samples containing three-dimensional structure or flame-retardant composition only illustrate slightly modified yet insufficient flame-retarding effect (Supplementary Fig. 16, Movie 15 and Note 2), demonstrating the respective contributions and synergetic effect of three-dimensional structures and TPP flame retardant for safe Li metal negative electrode. Thermal-gravimetric analysis (TGA) curves (Fig. 3h) indicate that after ZnO layer coating, the decomposition-releasing temperature of TPP in the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode is increased from ≤300℃ to gradual decomposition within the temperature range of 200 to 1200℃, which should be attributed to the low thermal conduction and high thermal dissipation effect of the porous electrode. This higher temperature, gradual decomposition and release of TPP in layered Li/ZnO/TPP/GO structure design can guarantee its stability during molten Li infusion fabrication step, and consistently deliver flame-retardant gases under ignition condition, which cannot be achieved by the attaching structure of Li@TPP/GO electrode (Supplementary Fig. 17). Numerous micro-scale holes generated on the surface of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode confirm the successful flame-retardant gases release during ignition 28 (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Fig. 18). COMSOL simulations demonstrate that high density flame-retarding gas can be in-situ, uniformly released from the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO and accumulate on the upper surface of electrode based on the gravity effect, while some flame-retarding gas can be adsorbed on the lower surface (Fig. 3j and Supplementary Movie 16), which is consistent with the observed flame-retardant gas diffusion behavior in realistic ignition condition (Supplementary Fig. 15). This gas-covering effect isolates the electrode from O2 atmosphere, effectively preventing the Li-O2 combustion reaction that cannot be realized by simply attaching Li foil to TPP/GO foam.

Last but not least, density functional theory (DFT) simulations illustrate the binding energy between Li atoms and PO· radicals (-3.15 eV, derived from TPP thermal decomposition 29) is much higher than that with O· radicals (-2.48 eV), supporting the prominent free Li atoms-capturing ability of PO· for interrupting the combustion chain reaction between Li and O2, thereby achieving the flame-retardant effect (Fig. 3k, Supplementary Fig. 19, Supplementary Data 1 and 2) 28-33. XRD pattern of the combustion products of the mixture of TPP and metallic Li and the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) depth profiles of the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode after ignition both display characteristic peaks of Li3PO4 (55.6 eV in Li 1s spectra, 133.6 eV in P 2p spectra and 531.4 eV in O 1s spectra 34,35), which is the reaction product of POS· with Li atom, supporting this flame-retardant mechanism (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21). In contrast, the XPS profiles of Li@TPP/GO and pure Li after ignition exhibit no Li3PO4-related peaks, because the TPP-derived phosphate composite (formed by the low decomposing temperature of flame retardant during the initial ignition) was carried away by thehot gas generated from the intense combustion of Li metal that last for several tens of seconds. In general, the smart-flame-retarding layered Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode design achieves good flame retardancy through the combined mechanisms of high thermal insulation/dissipation property of three-dimensional porous structure, the oxygen isolation effect of the in-situ released flame-retardant gas and the strong free Li atom-capturing ability of TPP-derived PO·. This provides strategies and mechanisms for solving the high combustion problem of Li metal negative electrode.

Battery performances during and after ignition condition

The flame-retarding property of the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode not only enables good resistance to Li metal combustion under ignition or heating conditions, but also enables the retention of Li negative electrode function after ignition. Before ignition, the pure Li negative electrode exhibits a specific capacity of 3591.81 mAh g-1 that is close to its theoretical capacity, while Li@TPP/GO illustrates a significantly decreased specific capacity of 1101.08 mAh g-1 that suggests severe corrosion reactions between metallic Li and TPP to deteriorate negative electrode fuction (Fig. 4a). After ignition, pure Li and Li@TPP/GO exhibit 0 remaining negative electrode capacity, proving all metallic Li was burned out toward full loss of the electrode function. In comparison, the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode only delivers a slightly decreased capacity from 2866.65 to 2459.99 mAh g-1 (85.81% electrode capacity reservation), demonstrating most of the Li negative electrode function was reserved after experiencing external ignition. Because of these significant differences in electrode function reservation, the symmetric Li||Li cell using after-burning Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrodes can support stable Li plating/stripping cycling for 1000 hours with an overpotential of ~100 mV in LP40FV electrolyte 36, while the after-burning pure Li and Li@TPP/GO electrode exceeded protection voltage at the beginning of the first charging process (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 22a). This suggests that Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrodes maintain stable Li stripping/plating negative electrode function even after ignition, which was also confirmed by the lower and stable charge transfer resistance of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode (7.774 Ω to 12.20 Ω through 100 to 300 cycles) than pure Li and Li@TPP/GO electrode (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 22b). In addition, the after-burning Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrodes also exhibit good rate performance at varying current densities (Supplementary Fig. 23). Top-view SEM images illustrate a uniform Li deposition morphology without any dendrites after 100 complete Li plating/stripping cycles in after-burning Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode (Supplementary Fig. 24). These results suggest that the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode well retained its Li metal negative electrode function after ignition.

Benefiting from the good flame retardancy of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode, the Li metal negative electrode-based full-cell can afford stable battery performance even during or after ignition. As shown in Fig. 4d, the Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NCM811) full-cell using after-burning Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode exhibits 93.72% capacity retention after 250 cycles at a specific current of 94 mA g-1 in LHCETTE electrolyte 37, with stable voltage profiles, coulombic efficiency and charge-transfer resistance (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Figs. 25 and 26). At the same time, this cell exhibits good rate performance of 88.26% capacity retention at 376 mA g-1 and 63.22% capacity retention at 940 mA g-1 (Supplementary Fig. 27). In comparison, the full-cell with after-burning pure Li negative electrode exhibits a rapid capacity decay to 36.03% after only 80 cycles, while the full cell using ignited Li@TPP/GO negative electrode shows a lower 35.08% capacity retention after only 50 cycles (Fig. 4f), along with significantly degraded rate performance. These comparisons prove the good flame-resistance and capacity retention ability when the electrode was ignited.

Owing to the good fire retardancy of our Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode, the Li metal pouch cell can afford a self-fire-extinguishing ability and supply energy output even when the battery core was exposed to fire. As shown in Fig. 4g, we evaluate the safety property by recording the light-emitting diode (LED)-powering function of a 100 mAh Li metal battery using non-flammable electrolyte (1 M LiPF6 in a mixture of fluoroethylene carbonate /3,3,3-fluoroethylmethyl carbonate/1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl ether (FEC:FEMC:HFE, 2:6:2 by weight)) 7 when the Li metal negative electrode in the battery core was exposed to external fire through the damage site in package (Supplementary Fig. 28 and Movie 17). Fig. 4h shows that the conventional Li metal pouch cell using pure Li negative electrode shows a severe combustion after only 2 seconds of ignition, rapidly spreading through the whole battery and lasting for more than 20 seconds to fully destroy the battery (Supplementary Movie 18). This represents an intense combustion issue to be more violent than conventional Li-ion battery (Supplementary Fig. 29 and Movie 19). Debris analysis in Supplementary Fig. 30 proves that the Li metal negative electrode, separator and package was all burned out, while the NCM811 positive electrode maintained the original morphology, suggesting the high safety issue of LMB should be attributed to the Li metal negative electrode. In comparison, the Li metal pouch cell employing Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode successfully keeps powering the LED without any combustion during three times of 2-second ignitions (Fig. 4i), or even a 20-second-lasting ignition (Supplementary Movies 20-23 and Supplementary Fig. 31). This good flame-retardant effect of the Li metal pouch cell should be attributed to our electrode design against lithium oxidation reaction, rather than the non-flammable electrolyte (Supplementary Table 2, Supplementary Figs. 33, 33 and Movies 24, 25) 38,39. Nail penetration test and accelerating rate calorimetry (ARC) measurement are conducted to further evaluate the battery's safety under realistic abuse conditions. During the nail penetration test, Li/ZnO/TPP/GO||NCM811 pouch cell exhibited neither visible smoke nor open flame that overwhelms the exploded pure Li metal negative electrode-based pouch cell (Supplementary Figs. 34 and 35). In ARC measurement, Li/ZnO/TPP/GO||NCM811 pouch cell demonstrated a high self-heating onset temperature (T1) of 176.37°C (versus 160.84°C for the pure Li system) and a reduced peak temperature (T3) of 352.97°C (versus 500.12°C for the pure Li system), and consistently lower temperature increasing rate (dT/dt ≤ 1.96℃ min-1) than the pure Li system (T2 = 295.67°C when dT/dt ≥ 100℃ min-1) (Supplementary Fig. 36 and Movies 26, 27) 40,41. These results indicate that our smart-flame-retard layered composite Li electrode design does successfully address the high combustibility problem of Li metal negative electrode, affording a fire-resistant, high safety Li metal battery with great significance for safe energy storage applications.

Electrochemical performances during regular battery operation

In addition to the good flame retardancy, the ZnO interlayer from layered host design also enables complete shielding of TPP dissolution-induced Li/TPP corrosion reaction, affording significantly improved Li negative electrode performance. As shown in Fig. 5a, the Li@TPP/GO electrode-based symmetric cell exhibits a greatly shortened cycle life (<100 hours) with unstable voltage profiles than pure Li negative electrode (800 hours), and the averaged 82.32% Li plating/stripping coulombic efficiency (CE) in TPP/GO host is also much lower than regular copper (98.81%, Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 37). This should be attributed to the dissolution of unprotected TPP into electrolyte and severe corrosion reaction between Li negative electrode and TPP. In contrast, the layered Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode-based symmetric cell exhibits stable voltage profiles with minimal hysteresis (1200 h with an overpotential of 97.5 mV). In the Li||host half-cell testing, the ZnO/TPP/GO host (after complete Li stripping from the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO) also illustrates a greatly improved Li plating/stripping CE of 99.06% and stable overpotentials ranging from 124.5 to 175.6 mV between 100 and 400 Li plating/stripping cycles. This improvement can also be observed in Aurbach's CE testing (Supplementary Fig. 38). These comparisons prove that our layered electrode design can successfully terminate the TPP dissolution and side reaction-induced Li negative electrode degradation issue, as further demonstrated by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) spectra and high-current, high-capacity symmetric cell cycling results (Supplementary Figs. 39 to 41). In addition, the high lithiophilic ZnO-converted LiZn coating layer 42 and three-dimensional structure 43 of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO can further improve the reversibility of Li negative electrode reaction, which is responsible for the higher performance than pure Li negative electrode. Based on these advantages, the Li metal||NCM811 full-cell using 4 mAh cm-2 Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode and 1.63 mAh cm-2 NCM811 positive electrode can deliver a 79.09% capacity retention after 500 cycles with stable voltage profiles at a specific current of 94 mA g-1, outperforming those of pure Li||NCM811 full-cell (79% retention after 233 cycles) and Li@TPP/GO||NCM811 full-cell (79% retention after only 125 cycles, Fig. 5c and Supplementary Figs. 42 and 43). The same negative: positive electrode capacity ratio (RN/P) of the three full cells was realized by completely stripping Li from Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode in half-cell, depositing 4 mAh cm-2 Li into negative electrode, dissembling from half-cell and assembling into the full-cells (Supplementary Figs. 44 and 45). EIS spectra and rate performance also illustrate significantly improved negative electrode kinetic from the layered host design (Supplementary Figs. 46 and 47). In the pouch cell with higher energy density, the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode still exhibits good cycle stability (Supplementary Figs. 48 and 49). These results prove that the our ZnO interlayer and layered host design can successfully solve the incompatibility and side reaction issue between flame retardant and Li metal negative electrode, constructing Li metal batteries with high safety and cycle stability.

The mechanisms of layered host design for suppressing Li-flame retardant corrosion reaction and improving negative electrode performance were revealed by characterizing SEI composition and deposited Li morphology. XPS depth profiles of Li@TPP/GO electrode shows high Li3PO4-related peaks in P 2p (133.6 eV) and Li 1s spectra (55.6 eV) 34,35, suggesting large amount of Li3PO4 species existed in the SEI of Li@TPP/GO negative electrode (Fig. 5d and e). Considering the absence of phosphorus-related elements in LHCETTE electrolyte, this result proves that TPP in the unprotected TPP/GO host was dissolved into electrolyte and corrode the Li metal negative electrode, while the generated Li3PO4-containing SEI is unfavorable for uniform Li deposition and reversible Li negative electrode operation 11,44. In comparison, the XPS depth profiles of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode illustrates full absence of Li3PO4-peaks (Fig. 5f and g), demonstrating that the ZnO interlayer design can completely seal the TPP component inside the interlayer of Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode during regular negative electrode cycling, preventing TPP from Li metal corrosion reactions and allowing the formation of a favorable LiF-dominant SEI 45-47 (Supplementary Figs. 50 to 52). In addition, our layered composite negative electrode design also avoids the flame-retardant dissolution-derived phosphors-containing positive electrode-electrolyte interphase, which is also beneficial for positive electrode cycling stability (Supplementary Figs. 53-55). Owing to the advantages of high-surface-area three-dimensional host structure 43 and the lithiophilic properties of ZnO-converted LiZn interlayer 42,48, lower nucleation and migration barriers are realized in the Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode. After 100 complete Li plating/stripping cycles, it illustrates the uniform, averaged 7.3 μm-diameter grain-sized Li deposition morphology (Fig. 5h and Supplementary Fig. 56), overwhelming the highly dendritic deposition morphology in pure Li (Fig. 5i) and Li@TPP/GO (Fig. 5j). These comparisons prove that the layered host design can successfully address the incompatibility and corrosion reaction challenge between Li metal and flame retardants, affording simultaneous achievement of high safety and long cycle life in Li metal battery.
paper_content.methods:
Preparation of the smart-flame-retarding layered host (ZnO/TPP/GO)

The TPP (Beijing InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd., the purity is 98%, used without any treatment) ethanol solution (Ordered from https://shop507945882. taobao.com/, the purity is 99%, used without any treatment) (0.125 g ml-1) and commercially available GO solution (Hangzhou Gaoxi Technology, 10 mg g-1, dispersed in water) were uniformly mixed according to the mass ratio of TPP to GO of 2:1. The mixed solution was coated on the plastic film (Ordered from https://shop36317712. taobao.com/, 24 cm length, 16 cm width) with a thickness of 750 μm using a doctor blade (Modern Instruments, GB-SZQ-1000), and dried at -20 ± 5℃ in a freeze-dryer (Henan Fujing Instrument and Equipment Co., Ltd., FK-04) for 24 h to form a porous TPP/GO foam. The foam was stripped from the film and sandwiched between two layers of polypropylene films (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-SE-002901 16 um), and calendared to 80 μm (for Li||host coin cells and Li||NCM811 coin cells) or 125 μm (for symmetric coin cells) with a roller press (Shenzhen KeJing Star Technology Co., Ltd., GMSK-2150) in an air atmosphere. The calendared TPP/GO foam was cut into circular foams with a diameter of 11.5 mm for symmetric coin cells, circular foams with a diameter of 15 mm for Li||host coin cells and Li||NCM811 coin cells using puncher (Ordered from https://shop 3S0350276. taobao.com/, 11.5 and 15mm diameter) and rectangular foam with dimensions of 5.7 cm × 4.5 cm using scissor in an air atmosphere. ZnO nanolayer was deposited into the foam using the atomic layer deposition machine (Xiamen Yunmao Technology Co., Ltd., Mini AL D system) at 150°C with diethyl zinc (DEZn, Nanjing ai mou yuan Scientific equipment Co., Ltd., 99.9999%, liquid) and deionized water (0.1 multiply 10^6 Ω*cm) as precursors. The source MFC carrier gas flow rate of DEZn and water were 60 SCCM and the source in times were 85 ms and 50 ms, with 3-seconds static transition and 20-seconds transition purge (using nitrogen gas (Jinan Deyang Special Gas CO., Ltd., purity is 99.999%)) to remove excess precursors after each pulse. Approximately 500 ALD cycles were needed to prepare the sample.

Preparation of the smart-flame-retarding layered composite Li electrode (Li/ZnO/TPP/GO)

In an argon-atmosphere glove box (Mikrouna (Shanghai) Ind. Int. Tech. Co., Ltd., H₂O and O₂ content < 0.01 ppm), approximately 0.1 grams of Li metal foil (Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd., the purity is 99.95%) was heated on a 350 ± 10℃ hotplate (purchased from DLAB Scientific Co., Ltd., MS7-H550-Pro) for 5 minutes. This Li metal foil was quickly melted into a molten Li droplet on the hotplate. After fully molten of the Li metal, the previously obtained ZnO/TPP/GO host was transferred onto the hotplate. By gently bringing the edge of the host into contact with the molten Li, rapid infiltration of the liquid metal throughout the host structure was achieved within 10 seconds. Measured by the balance (Shanghai Shunyu Hengping Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd. FA2004, the measuring range is 200 g, the accuracy is 0.1 mg.) in the glovebox, about 2.72 mg cm-2 Li was calculated to be infused into the host, detailed mass ratios of each component are shown in Supplementary Table 1. The obtained electrodes were naturally cooled to 25 ± 5℃ for battery assembly inside the glovebox.

Preparation of the Li@TPP/GO control electrode

The control electrode (Li@TPP/GO) was fabricated in an argon-atmosphere glovebox (Mikrouna (Shanghai) Ind. Int. Tech. Co., Ltd., H₂O and O₂ content < 0.01 ppm). A piece of pure Li foil was affixed to the pre-formed TPP/GO foam disc to construct the electrode. The Li foils with two kinds of areal capacities/sizes were used (purchased from Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd., the purity is 99.95%): 20 mAh cm⁻² (11.5 mm diameter) for symmetric cells and 4 mAh cm-² (15 mm diameter) for Li||NCM811 cells. The TPP/GO foam was correspondingly prepared as 11.5 mm or 15 mm discs as well. The finished electrode was stored within the glovebox at 25 °C ± 5 °C until battery assembly.

NCM811 positive electrode fabrication

The NCM811 positive electrode was fabricated by mixing 92% NCM811 powder (purchased from Nanjing Mojiesi Company, purity is 99%), 4% super carbon 65 (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-CO-0004, purity is 99.52%, average particle size is 150 nm), and 4% polyvinylidene difluoride binder (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-BI-0008, purity is 99.5%, molecular weight: ≥ 1.5 million) into N-methyl pyrrolidone (Beijing InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd., purity is 99.5%, water content≤50 ppm) with automatic planetary centrifugal vacuum stirring defoaming machine (Shenzhen Zhidi Technology Co., Ltd., ZD-T600C) for one hour at atmospheric environment with a temperature of 25 ± 5°C to prepare a slurry. The slurry was then coated onto both sides of carbon coated aluminum foil (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-CU-0003. The thickness and purity of carbon-coated layers were 1 μm and 99.5% respectively. The thickness and purity of the uncoated Al foil were 15 μm and 99.6% respectively.) at atmospheric environment with a temperature of 25 ± 5°C, and dried in a vacuum oven (Shanghai Yiheng Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6021, 133 Pa) at 60 ± 1℃ for 24 hours. The calculated theoretical areal capacity of the NCM811 electrode was around 4.29 mAh cm-2 per surface (about 250 μm thick). The electrodes were cut into 4.5 × 5.7 cm2 and stored in the glove box at 25 ± 5°C (Mikrouna (Shanghai) Ind. Int. Tech. Co., Ltd., water and O content <0.01 ppm) for pouch cell long cycle, nail penetration and accelerating rate calorimetry (ARC) test.

Construction and electrochemical characterization of coin cells.

All the coin cells (CR2032, 304 stainless steel, Canrd Co., Ltd.), comprising the case (CR2032, Canrd Co., Ltd.) spacer (15.8 mm × 1.0 mm, Canrd Co., Ltd.) and funnel spacer (15.4 mm × 1.1 mm, Canrd Co., Ltd.), were assembled in an argon-filled glovebox (Mikrouna (Shanghai) Ind. Int. Tech. Co., Ltd., H₂O and O₂ content < 0.01 ppm) using Celgard 2325 separators (Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-SE-000201 , porosity: 39%, avg. pore size: 0.028 μm, thickness: 25 μm, diameter: 19 cm). After assembly, the cells were allowed to rest for 24 hours at 25 ± 5°C prior to testing. All the subsequent electrochemical tests were conducted using a LAND battery test system (Wuhan Land Electronics Co., Ltd., CT3002A, 5 V, 1 mA & 10 mA 8C1U). During testing, the cells were placed in a constant-temperature environmental chamber (Wuhan Yueda Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., model YDC-300HT) maintained at 25.0 ± 0.2°C.

Symmetric coin cells were fabricated using either conventional or after-burning pure Li (20 mAh cm-², purchased from Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd., the purity is 99.95%), Li@TPP/GO or Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrodes (11.5 mm diameter). Two types of electrolytes were employed: LP40FV (1M LiPF₆ in EC/DEC with 10% FEC and 1% VC) and LHCETTE (LiFSI:DME:TTE=1:1.2:3). The LP40FV electrolyte was formulated by combining 89 wt% of a 1 M LiPF₆ solution in EC/DEC (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0202; H₂O content ≤ 20 ppm, used without further purification or treatment) with 10 wt% fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC, purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0893; purity is 99.95%, H₂O content≤ 50 ppm, used without further purification or treatment) and 1 wt% vinylene carbonate (VC, purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0892; purity is 99.9%, H₂O content ≤ 30 ppm, used without further purification or treatment). The LHCETTE electrolyte was prepared by mixing lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI, purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0832, purity is 99.5%, H₂O content ≤ 100 ppm, used without further purification or treatment), 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, purchased from Beijing InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd., purity is 99.5%, H₂O content ≤50 ppm, used without further purification or treatment), and 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE, purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., purity is 97%, pre-dried with 500 μm Li foil for 7 days until Li color stabilized). The components were mixed in a molar ratio of LiFSI:DME:TTE = 1:1.2:3. The Li plating/stripping stability of these symmetric cells was evaluated via galvanostatic cycling at current densities of 1.0 or 3.0 mA cm-² with capacity densities of 1.0 or 3.0 mAh cm-². Rate capability was tested by applying a sequence of current densities (0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and back to 0.5 mA cm-²), holding each for 10 cycles.

Li||host coin cells were fabricated with a working electrode consisting of either copper foil (Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-CU-000202; purity: 99.99%, thickness: 9 μm, diameter: 16 mm), TPP/GO foam (thickness: 80 μm, diameter: 15 mm), or a ZnO/TPP/GO host. The ZnO/TPP/GO host was obtained by electrochemically stripping Li completely from the pre-obtained Li/ZnO/TPP/GO electrode, using a charging current of 0.2 mA until a voltage of 0.2 V was reached. A pure Li foil (Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd.; purity: 99.95%, thickness: 500 μm, diameter: 11.5 mm) served as counter electrode, and 60 μL of LHCETTE electrolyte was used in each cell. The Coulombic efficiency (CE) of Li plating/stripping in the Li||host coin cells was determined by the ratio of discharging capacity to charging capacity. Furthermore, the long-term cycling stability of these cells was evaluated at a current density of 1 mA cm-², with a Li plating areal capacity set at 1 mAh cm-² and a Li stripping cut-off potential set at 150 mV. Additionally, Aurbach CE tests were conducted according to the following sequence: Deposite Li into the host (copper foil, TPP/GO foam or ZnO/TPP/GO host) at an area capacity of 5 mAh cm-2; Strip Li from it to a cut-off potential of 0.15 V; Deposite Li at 5 mAh cm-2 (capacity denoted as QA) again; Perform 10 cycles at a Li plating/stripping current density of 0.5 mA cm-2 and an areal capacity density of 0.5 mAh cm-2 (capacity denoted as QB); Strip Li to a cut-off potential of 0.15 V again (capacity denoted as QC). The average CE in Aurbach CE test was calculated using the formula: CE_average = (10QB + QC) / (10QB + QA)

Li||NCM811 coin cells were fabricated with the following components: NCM811 positive electrode (1.63 mAh cm-², purchased from Canrd Technology Co Ltd., SY33XX, punched into 12 mm discs using a manual slicer (Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Co., Ltd., MSK-T10)), 4 mAh cm-² pure Li (Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd., 99.95%), Li@TPP/GO or Li/ZnO/TPP/GO negative electrode, and 90 μL of ELHCETTE electrolyte. The pre-stripping/plating process was conducted at a constant current of 0.2 mA for both stripping and plating, with the stripping process terminated upon reaching a cut-off potential of 0.2 V. For initial activation, the full-cells were charged to 4.35 V and then discharged to 3.0 V at a specific current of 9.4 mA g-¹ for 2 cycles. Following activation, long-term cycling tests were carried out at a charge/discharge specific current of 94 mA g-¹. Rate capability was evaluated by varying the specific current in a sequence (37.6 - 94 - 188 - 376 - 564 - 940 - 564 - 376 - 188 - 94 - 37.6 mA g-¹), holding each for 5 cycles.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted with a CHI 760E electrochemical workstation. All tests were executed under potentiostatic conditions with an applied AC amplitude of 5 mV, scanning across a frequency spectrum of 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. To ensure a stable baseline, the system was held at the open-circuit voltage for 10 minutes prior to each measurement.

Fabrication of Li||NCM811 pouch cells for long cycle test

The Li||NCM811 pouch cells used for long cycle test were assembled using 4.5 × 5.7 cm2 NCM811 positive electrode (4.29 mAh cm-2 (one side)) and 10 mAh cm-2 pure Li (Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd., 99.95%) or Li/ZnO/TPP/GO in an argon-filled glovebox (Mikrouna (Shanghai) Ind. Int. Tech. Co., Ltd., water and O content <0.01 ppm) at 25 ± 5°C. The separator was 16 μm microporous polyethylene (PE) membrane (purchased from Canrd Technology Co Ltd.). The cell core was sealed in an aluminum plastic packing film (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-FC-001103), and LHCETTE electrolyte was injected into the pouch cell (by pipette) according to 2 g Ah-1, followed by sealing and gas releasing of the pouch cell using vacuum pre-sealing machine (Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Company, MSK-115A-III). These cells were rested for 24 hours before 37.6/56.4 mA g-1 charging/discharging cycling between 3.0 V and 4.5 V at 25 ± 0.2°C. No external pressure is applied during the battery cycling process.

Fabrication of pouch cells for ignition test

The Li||NCM811 and graphite||NCM811 pouch cells used for the ignition test were assembled using 4.5 × 5.7 cm 2 NCM811 positive electrode (3.82 mAh cm-2, purchased from Canrd Technology Co Ltd.) and 4.5 × 5.7 cm2 pure Li (Shandong Zhongshan Photoelectric Materials Co., Ltd., 99.95%), Li/ZnO/TPP/GO or graphite (purchased from Canrd Technology Co Ltd.) in an argon-filled glovebox (Mikrouna (Shanghai) Ind. Int. Tech. Co., Ltd., water and O content <0.01 ppm). The separator was 12 μm microporous polyethylene (PE) membrane (purchased from Canrd Technology Co Ltd., MA-EN-SE-0007). The cell core was sealed in an aluminum plastic packing film (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-FC-001103), and 0.25 mL all-fluorinated electrolyte (1 M LiPF6 (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0840, purity is 99.95%, water content ≤50 ppm, used without any treatment)in a mixture of fluoroethylene carbonate /3,3,3-fluoroethyl methyl carbonate/1,1,2,2-tetrafluoro ethyl-2,2,2-trifluoro ethyl ether (FEC (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0893, purity is 99.95%, water content ≤50 ppm, used without any treatment):FEMC (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0894, purity is 99.95%, water content ≤20 ppm, used without any treatment):HFE (purchased from Canrd Co., Ltd., MA-EN-ET-0874, purity is 99.9%, water content ≤20 ppm, used without any treatment), 2:6:2 by weight)) electrolyte was injected into the pouch cell (by pipette), followed by sealing and gas releasing of the pouch cell using vacuum pre-sealing machine (Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Company, MSK-115A-III). Before the ignition tests, these pouch cells were charged to 4.35 V at a specific current of 9.4 mA g-1 at 25 ± 0.2°C. No external pressure is applied during the battery charging process.

Safety performance test

The nail penetration test was carried out in a commercial nail penetration system (BE Nail Penetration Tester, BE-6047C-20T). A 5 mm diameter steel nail was driven at a speed of 25 mm s−1 through the Li metal pouch cells with 100% stage of charge (SOC). The thermal behavior of the Li metal pouch cells was characterized by an accelerating rate calorimeter (ARC HEL BTC-130) in a standard heat–wait–seek procedure.

Characterization

SEM images were taken with a scanning electron microscope (SEM, ZEISS EVD-18). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are collected with JEOL JEM-2100F. FIB-SEM images were taken through cross-sectioning sample with a Ga+ ion beam and observing with the electron beam on a focus ion beam-SEM (FIB-SEEM, Helios 5 CX). The composition of the samples was examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker AXS D2 Phaser X-ray powder diffractometer), Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). The XPS spectra of the SEI were measured by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo escalab xi+). The binding energies were calibrated with respect to the C 1s peak at 284.6 eV. All the cycled electrodes were rinsed with pure anhydrous DME solvent (purchased from Beijing InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd., purity is 99.5%, water content ≤50 ppm without any treatment) to remove residual LiFSI, dried, and then sealed in the glovebox at 25 ± 5°C before being transferred using a vacuum transfer vessel for SEM, TEM and XPS characterizations. The infrared thermal imaging videos was shot by Huajingkang K26E25 online infrared thermal camera at atmospheric environment with a temperature of 25 ± 5°C.

Computational method

COMSOL simulation: The heat transfer behavior of dense Li metal and foam Li metal under continuous flame was simulated by finite element method in a three-dimensional model. Specifically, the solid fluid heat transfer module in COMSOL was used for calculation. The heat transfer inside the Li metal and between the Li metal and the surrounding gas followed the Fourier heat transfer law. The gas around the Li metal was set as air. The solution process used the Hex-Dominant hexahedron grid method, and the relative tolerance was set to 1 e-6 to ensure the accuracy of the solution results.

The gas diffusion behavior in three-dimensional space around the smart-flame-retarding layered Li metal (Li/ZnO/TPP/GO) under flame was simulated by finite element method. Specifically, Ansys Fluent was used for parameter setting and flow field solving. The continuity equation, momentum equation and energy equation were followed in the fluid mechanics calculation process. The VOF model based on Euler-Euler method was used for the multiphase flow model between gas mixtures, and k-ω SST model was used for turbulence model. The inlet was set as a polyphase inflow port, defined as a mass inflow port. The outlet was a pressure outlet, and the outlet gauge pressure was 0 Pa. The solution process used the Hex-Dominant hexahedron grid method, and the relative tolerance was set to 1 e-6 to ensure the accuracy of the solution results.

Density functional theory: Based on Density functional theory (DFT) and the calculation method of quantum mechanics, the DMol module in Materials Studio software was used to calculate the binding energy. The single point energy of Li, O2, PO·, Li2O after Li combining with O2 and Li3PO4 after Li combining with PO· were calculated respectively, and the differences were obtained to obtain binding energies. The formula is as follows:
ΔE1 = ELi2O - (ELi + EO2) ; ΔE2 = ELi3PO4 - (ELi + EPO·)

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this work, the authors report a layered composite Li anode (Li||ZnO||TPP||GO) designed to mitigate the extreme
flammability of Li metal while maintaining its electrochemical functionality. They demonstrate that a ZnO interlayer prevents
side reactions between Li and the flame retardant (TPP) under normal operation, whereas upon ignition, thermally triggered
decomposition of TPP releases gases that act as a flame retardant, thereby ensuring complete non-combustibility and
improved cycling stability. However, several critical scientific aspects have not been sufficiently addressed. First, although
TPP is a well-known flame retardant and, it does not, by itself, provide sufficient originality. Moreover, the study does not
systematically examine how varying the TPP content relative to the electrolyte affects flame-retardant behavior, making it
difficult to assess the practical extinguishing effect in real cells. Second, real-cell combustion arises from both Li metal and
the flammable liquid electrolyte, but the pouch-cell experiments show no ignition at all, which weakens the credibility of the
results. Third, the explanation of the claimed transport properties and underlying mechanism is incomplete and requires
additional clarification. If TPP is truly sealed under ZnO during normal operation, rapid gas release on heating would
require a defined permeation pathway or a thermally induced opening in that layer. The manuscript presents this only through
simulation, with insufficient explanation of the actual experimental evidence. Fourth, Li metal has an intrinsic melting point
near 180 ℃. Yet the data show no melting or flow behavior, and this complete absence is not convincingly explained by the
presence of TPP, ZnO, or GO. Finally, the scalability and practical relevance of the ALD-based ZnO interlayer and the multi-
layer host architecture are not addressed at a level commensurate with the strength of the safety claims.
In summary, although the idea of integrating a sealed flame-retardant layer with a lithiophilic interlayer within a porous host
is interesting and the dataset is extensive, the materials advance is limited, the key mechanism is insufficiently supported,
and several headline claims appear overstated. Therefore, this manuscript is not suitable for publication in Nature
Communications. Suggestions for improvement are provided as follows:
1. Cell ignition stems not only from the lithium-metal anode but also from the flammable electrolyte. However, the developed
anode does not specify the amount of TPP relative to the electrolyte. Please quantify the TPP loading versus electrolyte
volume/mass and explain how varying TPP content influences the observed flame-retardant effect.
2. The anode is claimed to provide both structural flame-retardant behavior and chemical extinguishing via TPP, but the
current explanation does not clearly decouple these effects. Please clarify the respective contributions and operating
windows of the structural design and the TPP-based chemical mechanism.
3. While the flame-retardant mechanism of TPP is broadly known, the description of how TPP functions in the presence of
lithium metal is insufficient. Please provide additional rationale or evidence supporting the proposed mechanism under Li-
metal conditions.
4. Under normal conditions, TPP is described as residing between the ZnO interlayer and Li to suppress side reactions.
However, it remains unclear how TPP is released upon heating and how that release contributes to flame retardancy.
Please include additional experimental results and mechanistic explanation.
5. In general, TPP requires substantial chemical transformation and gas release before delivering a flame-retardant effect.
However, in this study, ignition was absent or extinguished almost immediately. Because TPP decomposition typically
needs time and elevated temperature, please explain why, in this design, TPP can act nearly instantaneously.
6. Lithium metal melts at ~180 ℃, a fundamental property that should persist regardless of structure. Yet no melting behavior
is reported here. Please provide the proposed mechanism and observations with Li’s intrinsic melting point.
7. ZnO and GO are designed to suppress electrochemical side reactions between TPP and Li. If so, TPP-related changes
should be consistently detectable after combustion without regard to ZnO or GO. However, post-ignition XPS for
Li@TPP||GO shows no phosphorus signal, unlike Li||ZnO||TPP||GO. Please explain in more detail how these post-
combustion analyses support the claimed flame-retardant action.
8. A pouch cell contains Li metal, a cathode, and a liquid electrolyte, and flammable electrolytes are major factor driver of
thermal runaway. Despite this, the pouch-cell tests showed no ignition. Please explain how electrolyte combustion was
prevented and comment on the robustness and reliability of the pouch-cell experiments.
9. Please discuss whether the proposed mechanism and results are realistically reproducible at large-format cell or pack
scales. Also elaborate on the design’s sufficiency for scale-up and integration into practical cells.
10. Given dataset limitations and the absence of certain key comparisons, please provide additional explanation to ensure
that safety and performance claims are not overstated.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This work by Qi et al. proposes a smart-flame-retarding layered host design for safe Li metal battery. This host achieves self-
fire-extinguishing function of Li metal anode even under extreme ignition conditions and completely seals the flame retardant
from Li metal corrosion for durable battery operation. Their design does solve the extreme flammability challenge of Li metal
anode that has hindered the practical application of lithium metal batteries for decades. Their anode flame-retardant effect,
especially for pouch cells which remained unignited after being continuously exposed to fire for 20 seconds, is very
impressive. Based on my research experience, there has never been any study that can address the flammability issue of Li
metal anode-everyone in this research field knows this serious concern, but nobody has ever solved it. This work is the first-
ever demonstration, so I believe this work will become a meaningful breakthrough in the whole Li metal battery field, giving
other scientists new ideas on how to address the safety issue of Li metal anode. Therefore, I strongly recommend
considering publishing this manuscript in Nature Communications, after addressing following comments:
1. From Supplementary Figure 8, the Li||ZnO||TPP||GO electrode still illustrates an excellent SET of 0 s/g even after a
sustained 10 seconds of constant ignition. This result can be more convincing if the authors provide infrared thermal images
of multiple repeating samples into supplementary information to further confirm this excellent effect.
2. As shown in Figure 4d, the Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NCM811) full-cell using after-burning Li||ZnO||TPP||GO anode
exhibits a significant improvement in capacity retention and cycle life. It would be better to present the CE comparison of the
three kinds of full-cells to further support this advantage.
3. In the full cells test under regular operating conditions, stripping Li completely from Li||ZnO||TPP||GO anode in half-cell is
the first step towards achieving the same RN/P of the three full cells. It would be better to conduct XRD tests on the host at
the fully stripped state for confirming the complete stripping of Li, thereby demonstrating the strict control of the RN/P.
4. Supplementary Figure 15 exhibits the uniform Li deposition morphology of after-burning Li||ZnO||TPP||GO electrode. But
SEM characterizations on the dendrites are known to be highly erratic. It would be better to add more reproducing SEM
characterization results for better supporting the authors‘ declaration.
5. The authors demonstrated that their design effectively promotes the uniform deposition of Li through the absence of
dendrites in Figure 5h. To confirm this effect, it would be best to conduct more reproducible SEM characterization and add
them into Supplementary Information.
6. The authors declare that the lithiophilic properties of ZnO-converted LiZn interlayer can facilitate uniform and dendrite-free
Li deposition. It would be better to cite more references and add some discussions to support this claim.
7. For a manuscript that primarily focuses on safety, it is necessary to include validation through tests such as pouch cell nail
penetration and accelerating rate calorimetry (ARC) measurements, in addition to ignition experiments.
8. Figure S16 should provide the equivalent circuit diagram used for impedance fitting, and Figure S16b should be
appropriately enlarged to improve the clarity of the manuscript.
9. The annotations within Figure S21 are incorrect (0.5 mA, 0.5 mAh). The author should revise them clearly or remove the
annotations altogether.
10. This manuscript focuses on anode protection, with the cathode playing a secondary role. However, comprehensive
characterization is essential for a high-level publication; therefore, appropriate cathode characterization should be included.
11. The protection of the lithium anode in this manuscript requires the introduction of a large number of inactive materials
such as GO, ZnO, and TPP. A major concern is whether the addition of these materials will significantly reduce the
gravimetric and volumetric energy densities of the lithium anode. The authors should provide detailed calculations to
address this issue.
12. The manuscript only presents combustion safety tests on pouch cells, but no performance evaluation. The authors
should supplement the work with long-cycle performance tests of high-energy-density pouch cells to enhance the impact of
the article.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
The authors are grateful to the reviewers for their constructive comments on the
original manuscript. All reviewers’ comments were carefully considered and
implemented/responded to in the revised manuscript. A detailed response is given for
each comment. We italicized the reviewers’ comments and suggestions and highlight
our responses in purple for clarity.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Comments:
In this work, the authors report a layered composite Li anode (Li||ZnO||TPP||GO)
designed to mitigate the extreme flammability of Li metal while maintaining its
electrochemical functionality. They demonstrate that a ZnO interlayer prevents side
reactions between Li and the flame retardant (TPP) under normal operation, whereas
upon ignition, thermally triggered decomposition of TPP releases gases that act as a
flame retardant, thereby ensuring complete non-combustibility and improved cycling
stability. However, several critical scientific aspects have not been sufficiently
addressed. First, although TPP is a well-known flame retardant and, it does not, by
itself, provide sufficient originality. Moreover, the study does not systematically
examine how varying the TPP content relative to the electrolyte affects flame-retardant
behavior, making it difficult to assess the practical extinguishing effect in real cells.
Second, real-cell combustion arises from both Li metal and the flammable liquid
electrolyte, but the pouch-cell experiments show no ignition at all, which weakens the
credibility of the results. Third, the explanation of the claimed transport properties and
underlying mechanism is incomplete and requires additional clarification. If TPP is
truly sealed under ZnO during normal operation, rapid gas release on heating would
require a defined permeation pathway or a thermally induced opening in that layer. The
manuscript presents this only through simulation, with insufficient explanation of the
actual experimental evidence. Fourth, Li metal has an intrinsic melting point near
180 ℃. Yet the data show no melting or flow behavior, and this complete absence is not
convincingly explained by the presence of TPP, ZnO, or GO. Finally, the scalability and
practical relevance of the ALD-based ZnO interlayer and the multi-layer host
architecture are not addressed at a level commensurate with the strength of the safety
claims.
In summary, although the idea of integrating a sealed flame-retardant layer with a
lithiophilic interlayer within a porous host is interesting and the dataset is extensive,
the materials advance is limited, the key mechanism is insufficiently supported, and
several headline claims appear overstated. Therefore, this manuscript is not suitable
for publication in Nature Communications. Suggestions for improvement are provided
as follows:
Response:
We thank you for the comments. We also thank the reviewer for many valuable
and constructive suggestions to improve our paper. In the following, we provide our
point-by-point responses to each of the comments.
Regarding your general comments, here we also provide several point-to-point
explanations for your comments as following:
(1) Reply to “although TPP is a well-known flame retardant and, it does not, by
itself, provide sufficient originality. Moreover, the study does not systematically
examine how varying the TPP content relative to the electrolyte affects flame-retardant
behavior, making it difficult to assess the practical extinguishing effect in real cells.”:
Regarding the reviewer’s originality concern, here we want to express that the
most important originality and novelty is the achievement of compatibility between the
flame retardant and metal Li in the electrode preparation and the battery cycling process,
as well as the smart flame-retardant effect of the Li metal anode, rather than the type of
the flame retardant. The originality of our works lies in the first-ever report of a self-
fire-extinguishing composite Li metal anode that withstands tens seconds of ignition by
our layered composite electrode design. Therefore, choosing TPP as the flame retardant
does not affect the originality of our work. In addition, the systematical study on how
varying the TPP content relative to the electrolyte affects flame-retardant behavior is
also added in this revision, as detailed discussed in the response to Comment 1.
(2) Reply to “real-cell combustion arises from both Li metal and the flammable
liquid electrolyte, but the pouch-cell experiments show no ignition at all, which weakens
the credibility of the results”:
Regarding this question, we would like to apologize that we do not emphasize
enough in our manuscript that the electrolyte we used in the pouch cells has already
been non-flammable (1 M LiPF in a mixture of fluoroethylene carbonate /3,3,3-
6
fluoroethylmethyl carbonate/1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl ether
(FEC:FEMC:HFE, 2:6:2 by weight), proposed by Fan et al. in Nature Nanotech, 2018,
13, 715–722, in both pure Li metal anode-based pouch cell and composite Li metal
anode-based pouch cell). This non-flammable electrolyte has a self-extinguishing time
of 0 s g-1 and exhibits excellent combustion suppression properties in lithium-ion
batteries. Therefore, the possibility of the electrolyte flammability is excluded, which
confirms the robustness and reliability of the pouch-cell experiments. Detailed
discussions are also added in the response to Comments 1 and 8.
(3) Reply to “the explanation of the claimed transport properties and underlying
mechanism is incomplete and requires additional clarification. If TPP is truly sealed
under ZnO during normal operation, rapid gas release on heating would require a
defined permeation pathway or a thermally induced opening in that layer. The
manuscript presents this only through simulation, with insufficient explanation of the
actual experimental evidence”:
Regarding this question, we add image capture of the digital videos into the
manuscript when the composite Li anode during annealing as strong evidence. These
images clearly capture releases of gas from the composite electrode upon heating. We
also add the SEM images and XPS characterizations of the ignited Li||ZnO||TPP||GO
electrode as strong evidences, showing newly appeared micrometer-scale pores and
flame retardant-derived phosphate-containing surface that support the mechanism of
flame-retardant release from inside the electrode to the surface. Detailed discussions
are also added in the response to Comment 4. We believe these new experimental results
and discussions can prove strong evidence for our claim.
Supplementary Figure 15. Digital photos of the flame-retarding gas released during
continuous ignition of Li||ZnO||TPP||GO electrodes (a-c) and Li||ZnO||TPP||GO ||
NCM811 pouch cells (d-f).
(4) Reply to “Li metal has an intrinsic melting point near 180 ℃. Yet the data
show no melting or flow behavior, and this complete absence is not convincingly
explained by the presence of TPP, ZnO, or GO”:
Regarding this question, we provide explanations from two aspects: Firstly, the
three-dimensional aerogel structure of the host with high thermal dissipation effect can
reduce the thermal conductivity of the electrode, thereby delaying the temperature
increasement inside the electrode compared to the ignition site and the melting of the
internal Li metal. Secondly, the three-dimensional structure of the host with high
lithiophilicity can adhere the locally melted Li metal against liquid flow, thereby the
phenomenon of flowing liquid-state molten Li metal cannot be observed. We also add
an infrared temperature distribution mapping image of the electrode after being ignited
for 10 seconds and a magnified plot of the DSC curve of the electrode to prove the
delay of temperature increasement and the actual occurrence of Li melting. Detailed
discussions are also added in the response to Comment 6.
(5) Reply to “the scalability and practical relevance of the ALD-based ZnO
interlayer and the multi-layer host architecture are not addressed at a level

We thank the reviewer for raising this suggestion. Following the reviewer’s
suggestion, we clarify the respective operating windows and contributions of the
structural design and the TPP-based chemical mechanism. At the beginning of the
ignition test (around 5 seconds), only the thermal insulation effect of the three-
dimensional structure was effective to prevent the thermal conduction to the whole
electrode, which is evidenced by the relatively lower temperature of most parts in the
electrode (except the ignition site) (Supplementary Fig. 10). After several seconds of
ignition, as the temperature gradually reached the decomposition temperature of TPP
(at about 200 ℃) at the ignition site, the thermal decomposition and release of TPP-
based flame retarding reaction start to take effect, and work together with three-
dimensional structure to exert the flame-retardant effect.
To clarify the respective contributions of the structural design and the TPP-based
chemical mechanism, we conducted ignition tests on the electrodes that only have a
three-dimensional structure but do not contain TPP (Li||ZnO||GO in Supplementary Fig.
7), as well as those that contain TPP but do not have a three-dimensional structure
(Li@TPP||GO in Supplementary Fig. 7). As clearly shown and compared in the
Supplementary Movies, the pure Li start to burn after 0.9 seconds of ignition (Fig. 3c
and Supplementary Movie 9), while the three-dimensional Li||ZnO||GO electrode start
to burn after 5.5 seconds of ignition due to the low thermal conduction and high thermal
dissipation properties (Supplementary Fig. 16 and Movie 15), while the TPP-containing
Li@TPP||GO electrode starts to burn after 0.5 seconds of ignition with clear observation
of TPP-derived smoke (Fig. 3d and Movie 10). In terms of self-extinguishing time
(SET), the average SET values of the two kinds of control electrodes are 691.76 and
744.31 s g-1 respectively, which are also lower than pure Li metal (979.27 s g-1). Due to
the absence of the TPP-based non-flammable gas release/free radical capture functions
in the former electrode and the absence of heat transfer delay effect provided by the
three-dimensional structure in the later electrode, neither of these two control electrodes
can achieve a satisfactory fire-retardant effect. These results demonstrate the respective
contributions and synergetic effect of three-dimensional structures and TPP flame
retardant for safe Li metal anode.

can be directly observed through the images during the ignition process

phenomenon of flowing liquid-state molten Li metal cannot be observed in the image.

into Supplementary Fig. 13, which illustrate a clear endothermic peak that prove the
actual happening of Li metal melting.
